items.title: Patient outcomes after simulation are not shown
items.whyItMatters: Admissions did not change in the best study and death was too rare to compare (claim c1).
items.opportunity: Keep time to first critical intervention primary and report admissions and deaths descriptively.

items.title: Checklist scores are poor proxies
items.whyItMatters: Simulation scores correlated weakly with real calls (claim c2).
items.opportunity: Measure real calls; keep simulation scores secondary.

items.title: Four clusters
items.whyItMatters: Few hospitals give imprecise estimates and few degrees of freedom (claim c4).
items.opportunity: Use a stepped design with calendar-time adjustment and small-sample corrections, and explain hospital differences qualitatively.

items.title: Families and patients with limited English in rapid response calls
items.whyItMatters: Families describe confusion about roles; those with limited English are least able to raise concern.
items.opportunity: Include families, with interpreters, in the qualitative sample and a family communication step in scenarios.

items.title: Ward staff anxiety about unannounced simulation
items.whyItMatters: 41 percent of ward nurses reported anxiety elsewhere (claim c3).
items.opportunity: Announce the programme, use signage and a stop word, and explore anxiety in interviews.

errorsFound: The need lists death within 24 hours as an outcome; it is too rare to compare between phases and should be a balancing measure.
reevaluation: The gaps confirm a stepped mixed methods design with a real-call primary outcome, patient outcomes described, and a qualitative strand to explain hospital differences.
summary: Five gaps; missing patient outcome evidence and weak proxies are high severity.
